name: Recording yourself

card.summary: Recording your voice or video to hear and see how you come across, then refine delivery.

quick.overview:
Recording yourself means capturing audio or video and reviewing it for feedback on voice, pace and presence.

People do it with a phone, repeat it over weeks and compare takes to see progress.
quick.mechanism: Playback gives the listener's view of your voice. Your own voice sounds deeper to you because of bone conduction, which recordings do not include.
quick.risks: Low risk. Many people find the first playback uncomfortable because of the difference from their internal voice.

lead: Recording yourself means capturing audio or video of your own speech and movement and reviewing it. In looksmaxxing circles it is used mainly for voice and presence: hearing how pitch, pace, clarity and filler words sound to others, spotting monotone stretches, and refining delivery over repeated takes. Some people also film themselves to review posture and gestures.[2][3]

Speakers often find their recorded voice sounds different from the voice they hear while talking. Because sound also travels through the skull to the inner ear, which favours lower frequencies, a person's own voice seems deeper and fuller to them than to listeners; a recording captures only the airborne sound.[1][3] Reviewing recordings gives an outside view that practitioners use alongside rehearsal and feedback from others.[2]
Voice and speech clinicians describe recordings as a practical self-evaluation tool when used for specific questions rather than overall judgments of how a voice sounds.[3]

chain: Hear and see how you come across
Adjust pace, pitch variation, clarity and posture
angle.text: Playback gives the listener's view of your voice and body language. People use it to refine delivery, such as pacing, vocal variety and clarity, and to check posture and gestures on video.

infobox: Pitch, pace, clarity, filler words, posture [2][3]
Bone conduction adds low frequencies to the voice you hear internally [1][3]

paras: People record short speech samples, calls or readings and listen back, noting pace, volume, monotone stretches and filler words. Some also film themselves to review posture and gestures. Public-speaking organisations use evaluation and feedback as a central training method, with members critiquing each other's speeches.[2]

The mismatch between how a voice sounds internally and on playback is sometimes called voice confrontation, and arises because bone conduction adds low-frequency resonance that recordings lack.[1] A Toronto speech therapy clinic adds that familiarity plays a part, since people hear their internal voice constantly but their recorded voice only occasionally, and that phones, laptop microphones, echo and background noise all shape how a recording sounds.[3]

The clinic suggests asking specific questions such as whether every word is understandable, judging one feature at a time, and noting what worked before what to improve. It lists pace, pitch variation and stress, clarity and steady volume as features to listen for, and suggests recording 30 to 60 seconds, reviewing once, choosing one area, and re-recording to compare.[3] It also says lasting or uncomfortable voice changes should be assessed by a doctor or speech-language pathologist.[3]
No studies found on self-recording as a looks or voice-improvement practice.
